summary: Discovery focused on Ember Payments' p95 latency SLOs, concurrency and streaming requirements. Customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for production fraud-detection and realtime scoring. Agreed next step: run benchmarks with sample payloads; Redwood to send pricing and security docs.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, and I have Liam from our SE team. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Rosa Alvarez: Good thanks, Rosa here. A little late on my end but ready.
[00:10] Samir Patel: Samir, engineering lead. We really wanna dig into p95 numbers and how you handle concurrency with streaming.
[00:17] Liam Chen: Great, that's our sweet spot. Quick agenda: understand your traffic profile, p95 targets, whether streaming is required for user flow, and then map to Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.
[00:26] Avery Kim: Also curious about cost tradeoffs, quantization and token/sec.
[00:29] Maya Patel: Perfect. Rosa, can you give a quick primer on the Ember workloads?
[00:34] Rosa Alvarez: Sure. We do realtime scoring for transactions, fraud signals and risk decisions. Average request is about 150 tokens, but we have lots of short ones too (30-50 tokens) for behavioral checks. Peak concurrency right now reaches about 800 concurrent requests for certain markets, global traffic. Our target p95 for decisioning is 120ms end-to-end, but we can tolerate up to 250ms in worst case for non-blocking flows. Long term, want sub-100ms p95 for core checks.
[00:57] Liam Chen: That's helpful. Quick clarifying: when you say p95 120ms, is that model infer latency or end-to-end including network + preprocessing?
[01:03] Rosa Alvarez: That's end-to-end as seen by the service. For model only, we need around 70-80ms p95 for the most critical flow.
[01:10] Samir Patel: And concurrency — 800 is peak. Steady-state more like 250-300. We do spikes in US evenings.
[01:17] Maya Patel: Good. Typical Redwood question: are you open to batching or is every request strictly single-shot? Any streaming?
[01:23] Jordan Lee: For the fraud path we need streaming for some flows since the UI shows progressive results — low-latency token streaming improves UX. But core scoring is single-shot, low-latency.
[01:33] Liam Chen: Okay so mixed workload: single-shot low-latency p95 target ~70-80ms model-only; streaming for progressive UI where token/sec throughput and incremental latency matter. Makes sense.
[01:43] Avery Kim: What's the difference in behavior between Hosted and Dedicated here? We're trying to understand risk of noisy neighbors.
[01:48] Maya Patel: Hosted is multitenant but we provide verified performance profiles and SLAs for paid tiers. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools, predictability, and isolation — less variance at p95. Private is for VPC/on-prem when you need full network control and customer-managed keys. For sub-100ms p95 at 800 concurrency, Dedicated is often the sweet spot, or Hosted with guaranteed capacity reservation — depends on cost.
[02:09] Rosa Alvarez: Any numbers you can share for tokens/sec or p95 for typical models?
[02:13] Liam Chen: Sure — rough numbers: for a 7B style model quantized (4-bit/8-bit), on a A100-like GPU, you might see ~30-60 tokens/sec depending on seq length and KV cache hit rate. For p95 latencies, with optimized kernels and CPU to GPU routing, model-only p95 for short sequences can be sub-100ms single-shot when you have dedicated capacity. But important caveat: actuals depend on sequence distribution, batching strategy, and whether streaming introduces overhead.
[02:38] Samir Patel: We have a lot of 150-token requests. How does batching affect p95?
[02:43] Liam Chen: Batching increases throughput but can increase tail latency if you wait to collect batch. Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching with latency SLOs — you can set a max latency budget (e.g., 20ms) so it'll only wait that long to fill a batch. Also prefix caching helps if many requests share prompts. In practice you tune batch size and wait to hit token/sec targets without violating p95.
[03:02] Rosa Alvarez: If we go Dedicated, how do autoscaling and burst work for spikes? We can't overprovision forever.
[03:08] Maya Patel: Dedicated offers configurable autoscaling and burst capacity. You can set base reserved nodes for steady-state and allow short bursts to a larger pool. We can model your spike profile — e.g., 250 steady, 800 peak — and recommend a commit that balances cost and SLOs.
[03:20] Jordan Lee: Network: we need VPC peering and private IPs. Any constraints on that?
[03:24] Liam Chen: For Dedicated we support VPC peering and private endpoints; Private deployment gives you full on-prem or VPC control. For Hosted you can use private link options in some regions. We'll share the network playbook.
[03:33] Samir Patel: Security: SOC2, audit logs, KMS? We need to know how keys are managed.
[03:38] Maya Patel: We have SOC2 Type II, support customer-managed KMS (bring-your-own-key) for Private and Dedicated; Hosted supports envelope encryption and Redwood KMS with strict controls. Audit logs and token-level tracing available in the Console. We'll share SOC2 and KMS docs.
[03:52] Rosa Alvarez: Great. Benchmarks: we want Redwood to run token/sec and p95 tests on our traces versus our in-house infra and maybe Anthropic/OpenAI.
[03:59] Liam Chen: We can run a Redwood-managed benchmark. We'll ask you to provide sample request traces — distribution of seq lengths, concurrency patterns, and payloads — and we'll run runs for Hosted and Dedicated. We can also simulate streaming patterns.
[04:13] Avery Kim: What tooling do you use for benchmarking? Is there a script we can run too?
[04:17] Liam Chen: Yes, we have a benchmark playbook and scripts — we'll share a token/sec load generator. It outputs p50/p95/p99 and token/sec. We typically run both inference-only and end-to-end (with network sim).
[04:28] Samir Patel: Do you support KV/prefix caching? We have a lot of repeated prompts for behavioral scoring.
[04:32] Liam Chen: Yes, prefix/KV cache support is built in. Cache hit rates can drastically reduce cost and latency for repeated patterns. We'll need to see your traces to estimate hit rate.
[04:41] Rosa Alvarez: Pricing question: how much more is Dedicated vs Hosted for reserved commit?
[04:45] Maya Patel: Pricing variables: committed capacity, instance type, region. As a ballpark, Dedicated commit pricing tends to be 2-3x unit cost compared to best-effort Hosted but you get predictable throughput and lower p95 variance. We'll send a tailored proposal.
[04:58] Jordan Lee: For Private, do we need to bring hardware or do you ship a package?
[05:02] Liam Chen: Private has two flavors: customer-managed infra (you provide hardware in your cloud/on-prem) or Redwood-assisted appliance for some enterprise customers. We'll scope that separately.
[05:10] Samir Patel: Operationally, what observability do we get? Token-level breakdown? Traces?
[05:14] Maya Patel: Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and tracing hooks. You can export logs to your SIEM. We also have regression alerts tied to eval prompts.
[05:25] Rosa Alvarez: One concern: streaming often increases p95 because each chunk flush has overhead. Can you give example numbers?
[05:32] Liam Chen: Streaming overhead depends on chunk size and transport. If you stream every 4 tokens you add more framing/transport overhead; bigger chunks reduce overhead but increase time-to-first-token. For progressive UI we tune chunk size and show partial tokens. In Dedicated we've seen streaming end-to-end p95 in the 120-200ms range for shorter sequences versus single-shot lower but less progressive UX.
[05:54] Maya Patel: I'd like to propose a benchmark matrix: 1) Single-shot model-only p95 at steady concurrency (250); 2) Single-shot at peak concurrency (800) with Dedicated autoscale; 3) Streaming run simulated with your UI chunking pattern; 4) Evaluate cache hit benefit. We'll run both Hosted reserved and Dedicated.
[06:12] Samir Patel: Sounds good. Are there standard models you recommend for our scoring? We currently have a fine-tuned 7B and are evaluating a 13B variant.
[06:20] Liam Chen: 7B quantized often gives best cost/latency balance. 13B gives quality lift but higher latency. For sub-100ms p95 at 150 tokens, 7B quantized on Dedicated is more feasible. We'll include model recommendations.
[06:33] Rosa Alvarez: How long to get a dedicated pilot up?
[06:36] Maya Patel: If we have traces, we can size and spin up pilot seats in 1-2 weeks. Full production commit depends on procurement.
[06:42] Avery Kim: Procurement: we'll need security artifacts, contract terms, and SLA numbers.
[06:47] Maya Patel: We'll send SOC2, DPA template, SLAs and pricing.
[06:51] Rosa Alvarez: Quick question — can Dedicated fall back to Hosted during maintenance? We can't have downtime.
[06:56] Liam Chen: Yes, Redwood supports fallback routing policies — can failover to compatible model variants or Hosted endpoints for short periods. Fallback adds latency but preserves availability.
[07:06] Samir Patel: For the benchmark, can you run both quantized and unquantized? We want to see quality/latency tradeoff.
[07:11] Liam Chen: Absolutely — we'll include FP16, 8-bit and 4-bit quant profiles where supported and measure quality with your eval prompts.
[07:20] Jordan Lee: Network: we'll need to confirm egress patterns and IP whitelisting for the Redwood benchmark runner.
[07:25] Maya Patel: Noted — we'll provide the runner IP ranges and a secure upload for traces.
[07:29] Rosa Alvarez: Any gotchas around compliance with EU data residency? We have EU customers.
[07:33] Maya Patel: We have region-aware routing and can pin workloads to EU region; Private deployments give you full residency. We'll include region options in the proposal.
[07:41] Avery Kim: Ok, time check — 15 minutes left?
[07:44] Maya Patel: Yes, let's quickly recap and assign next steps.
[07:48] Liam Chen: Recap: 1) Ember needs model-only p95 ~70-80ms and end-to-end p95 120ms target; 2) Mixed workload with streaming & single-shot; 3) Peak concurrency 800, steady 250; 4) Redwood to run benchmarks (Hosted reserved + Dedicated); 5) Redwood to send pricing, SOC2/KMS docs; 6) Ember to send traces and p95 doc.
[08:12] Rosa Alvarez: That matches our notes.
[08:15] Samir Patel: Quick clarification — for token/sec, will you surface tokens/sec per GPU and total cluster?
[08:20] Liam Chen: Yes, benchmark output shows tokens/sec per device, cluster total, p50/p95/p99 latencies, and streaming metrics (time-to-first-token, chunk latency).
[08:32] Jordan Lee: For the VPC peering, after we confirm, do you need any additional topology info?
[08:37] Maya Patel: We'll send a checklist: CIDR ranges, firewall rules, egress ports.
[08:42] Rosa Alvarez: Okay let's lock a date for the benchmark. How soon can you run it?
[08:46] Liam Chen: If you send traces by Friday (2026-03-06), we can schedule a run the week of March 9th. Results in 2-3 business days after run.
[08:55] Maya Patel: Action items we'll follow-up in email. Anything else?
[08:58] Avery Kim: No, looks good.
[09:00] Rosa Alvarez: Thanks everyone. Looking forward to the proposal.
[09:03] Maya Patel: Thanks all, we'll follow up with next steps and the benchmarking playbook. Bye.
[09:07] (call ends)

Notes on transcript fidelity: occasional mis-attributed lines and small transcription errors; timestamps approximate.
notes: Call included AE+SE from Redwood. Customer emphasized sub-100ms p95 model-only requirement and 800 peak concurrency. Agreed to benchmark. Redwood to provide pricing, security docs, and benchmark scripts. Customer to provide traces and p95 doc.
